name: Cute Sequences
description: Given a positive integer $$$m$$$, we say that a sequence $$$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$$$ of positive integers is $$$m$$$-cute if for every index $$$i$$$ such that $$$2 \le i \le n$$$ it holds that $$$x_i = x_{i - 1} + x_{i - 2} + \dots + x_1 + r_i$$$ for some positive integer $$$r_i$$$ satisfying $$$1 \le r_i \le m$$$. You will be given $$$q$$$ queries consisting of three positive integers $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$ and $$$m$$$. For each query you must determine whether or not there exists an $$$m$$$-cute sequence whose first term is $$$a$$$ and whose last term is $$$b$$$. If such a sequence exists, you must additionally find an example of it.
input_specification: The first line contains an integer number $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 10^3$$$) — the number of queries. Each of the following $$$q$$$ lines contains three integers $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le a, b, m \le 10^{14}$$$, $$$a \leq b$$$), describing a single query.
output_specification: For each query, if no $$$m$$$-cute sequence whose first term is $$$a$$$ and whose last term is $$$b$$$ exists, print $$$-1$$$. Otherwise print an integer $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \leq 50$$$), followed by $$$k$$$ integers $$$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i \le 10^{14}$$$). These integers must satisfy $$$x_1 = a$$$, $$$x_k = b$$$, and that the sequence $$$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k$$$ is $$$m$$$-cute. It can be shown that under the problem constraints, for each query either no $$$m$$$-cute sequence exists, or there exists one with at most $$$50$$$ terms. If there are multiple possible sequences, you may print any of them.
approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1166D — Cute Sequences [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
